must_remember: Brewster's Law states that $\tan(i_p) = n$, where $i_p$ is the polarizing angle and $n$ is the refractive index.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular to each other.
Malus's Law dictates that the transmitted intensity through an analyzer is $I = I_0 \cos^2(\theta)$.
Unpolarized light passing through an ideal polarizer has its intensity reduced to half ($I = \frac{1}{2} I_0$).
Anisotropic crystals like calcite and quartz exhibit double refraction, splitting incident light into an ordinary ray (O-ray) and an extraordinary ray (E-ray).
In negative crystals like calcite, the velocity of the extraordinary ray is greater than that of the ordinary ray ($v_e > v_o$).
In positive crystals like quartz, the velocity of the ordinary ray is greater than that of the extraordinary ray ($v_o > v_e$).
Circularly polarized light requires two mutually perpendicular plane-polarized beams of equal amplitude with a phase difference of odd multiples of $\pi/2$.
A quarter-wave plate introduces a phase difference of $\pi/2$ (or path difference of $\lambda/4$) between the O-ray and E-ray.
A half-wave plate introduces a phase difference of $\pi$ (or path difference of $\lambda/2$) between the O-ray and E-ray.

glossary.meaning: The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
Law stating that the intensity of plane-polarized light transmitted through an analyzer varies as the square of the cosine of the angle between their transmission axes.
The phenomenon where an unpolarized ray entering an anisotropic crystal splits into two refracted rays: O-ray and E-ray.
The refracted ray inside a birefringent crystal that obeys ordinary laws of refraction and travels with the same speed in all directions.
The refracted ray inside a birefringent crystal that does not obey Snell's law and whose speed depends on the direction of propagation.
An optical device made of a birefringent crystal cut parallel to the optic axis that introduces a phase difference of $\pi/2$ between O-ray and E-ray.
An optical device that introduces a phase difference of $\pi$ between O-ray and E-ray, capable of rotating the plane of polarization.
The property of certain materials to selectively absorb one of the mutually perpendicular components of polarized light while transmitting the other.
A synthetic sheet containing microscopic quinine iodosulfate crystals oriented in a plastic matrix used to produce polarized light.
A measure of the proportion of polarized light in a partially polarized beam, defined by $V = \frac{I_{max} - I_{min}}{I_{max} + I_{min}}$.
